04 · Read & review

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Emma received an email from the newspaper archivist. The staff had checked the entry called “Student Travel — decision not received”. They could confirm that it came from the October 2011 correspondence index. They could not give Emma the letter or the writer’s name.

“The words in the index were written by newspaper staff,” the archivist explained. “We don't know whether they are the writer's exact words.”

Emma thanked her. It was important. She had almost treated the title as a sentence from a student. Now she knew it was a description made by someone else.

She called Sarah.

“So we still don't know what happened?” Sarah asked.

“We know a letter was listed under that subject. We don't know who wrote it, what it said, or whether a decision really failed to arrive.”

The archivist offered one more piece of information. The entry was dated 12 October 2011. This was after Claire disappeared, but the date alone did not connect the letter to her case.

Later Fiona Bell sent Emma another message. The trust's records team had not found a confirmed record of returned decision letters. They had, however, found a blank form headed “Contact attempt”. It had spaces for a reference number, a date and a note about the action taken.

“Does that mean the trust called students who did not receive letters?” Emma asked.

“No,” Fiona said. “It tells us what staff could record. We haven't found a completed form.”

Emma placed the blank form beside the office manual. Both explained how staff were supposed to deal with problems. Neither showed that they had used the procedure in a particular case.

Sarah suggested that Emma ask the archive to identify the October writer. Emma disagreed. She wanted to understand the evidence without exposing anyone's private details.

Instead she asked whether the archive could confirm how many entries about the travel scheme appeared in the index, without sharing names or letter contents. The archivist said staff would check, but did not promise a complete count.

That evening Emma looked again at her four headings: Prepared, Sent, Received, Able to appeal. The new date helped her place a document in time, but it did not fill any of the missing columns.

She wrote her next question below them: If a notice was not received, how would anyone know that the fourteen-day review period had begun?

She closed the notebook. It was a fair question. It was not yet an accusation.
